title: Upper GI bleeding
subtitle: Resuscitate, risk-stratify, scope

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding in over 16s: management (CG141/NG24 series)
Diagnosis and management of nonvariceal upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage: guideline update
Baveno VII consensus on portal hypertension

red_flags.text: Haematemesis with shock, or fresh melaena with a tachycardia at rest.
Known varices, cirrhosis, or stigmata of chronic liver disease with any bleed.
Ongoing haematemesis with a reduced conscious level. This is an airway problem before it is a bleeding problem.
A bleed on anticoagulation, or a bleed after aortic surgery or with an aortic graft: think aorto-enteric fistula.
Rebleeding after endoscopic therapy. The second bleed carries a far higher mortality than the first.

do_now.text: Two large-bore cannulae, bloods, crossmatch, and activate the major haemorrhage protocol for shock.
Protect the airway in an actively vomiting or obtunded patient before anything else. Aspiration kills more often than exsanguination here.
Transfuse to a restrictive target in the absence of massive haemorrhage or cardiac ischaemia; liberal transfusion worsens outcome in variceal bleeding.
Suspected variceal bleed: start a splanchnic vasoconstrictor and antibiotic prophylaxis immediately, before endoscopy.

assess.text: Calculate a pre-endoscopy risk score. A very low score identifies the patient who can be managed without admission.
Distinguish variceal from non-variceal on history and examination: alcohol, known liver disease, jaundice, ascites, splenomegaly, caput.
Drug history: anticoagulants, antiplatelets, non-steroidal anti-inflammatories, steroids, and any recent change of dose.
Post-endoscopy risk stratification once the lesion is seen.
In known liver disease, quantify the reserve because it drives everything that follows.

investigate.text: FBC, U&E, LFT, coagulation, group and crossmatch, venous gas with lactate. A raised urea with normal creatinine suggests a substantial upper bleed.
Upper GI endoscopy within 24 hours of admission for all, and immediately after resuscitation for unstable patients.
CT angiography for continued bleeding when endoscopy has failed or cannot localise the source.
Ultrasound abdomen when varices are suspected and the liver history is unclear.

resuscitate.text: Correct coagulopathy according to the agent involved and the local reversal protocol; do not withhold reversal awaiting endoscopy in a shocked patient.
Platelet transfusion for active bleeding with a low count; fibrinogen replacement in massive haemorrhage.
Proton pump inhibitor after endoscopy in non-variceal bleeding with high-risk stigmata. Routine pre-endoscopy use does not change outcome.
Balloon tamponade only as a bridge in uncontrolled variceal bleeding, with a definitive plan already agreed.

definitive.text: Endoscopic haemostasis is the definitive treatment for most upper GI bleeds: dual therapy for a bleeding ulcer, band ligation for oesophageal varices.
Interventional radiology embolisation for rebleeding after failed endoscopic therapy, where available.
Surgery for uncontrolled bleeding when endoscopy and radiology have failed or are unavailable: under-run the vessel, and address the cause.
Early transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt in selected high-risk variceal bleeds, decided with hepatology.

escalate.text: Endoscopist and anaesthetist together for the unstable patient. An unprotected airway in an actively bleeding patient is not an endoscopy list problem.
Critical care for shock, rebleeding, or a patient needing airway protection for endoscopy.
Hepatology and interventional radiology early in variceal bleeding, not after the second bleed.

notes: Risk scores here are unusually useful: they identify both the patient who can go home and the patient who must not leave the resuscitation room.
The surgical role in upper GI bleeding is now small and late. Knowing when to call it is the skill.
Rebleeding is the event that changes the prognosis. Anticipate it before it happens rather than reacting when it does.
